beats.narration_text: A Skill isn't a plugin or an API — it's a folder. This one is called ip-clause-review, and inside it is a single file, SKILL.md, written in plain English. That file is the whole program: the checks, the order, what to flag. The choice is deliberate — text you can read is text you can audit, no hidden logic sitting where the reviewer can't see it.

The checks live in a Steps section — a numbered list Claude runs top to bottom. Read the file, apply each check to the clause, return the result. No branching, no jumping ahead, unless a step itself says otherwise. What that buys you is repeatability: the same clause fed in twice goes through the same list, and the list can't quietly change its mind between runs.

production_viz.label: READ, CHECK, RETURN
production_viz.caption: linear — no branching unless a step says so

beats.narration_text: One item on the list is the ownership check. Here's what's actually happening: a clause that grants a license just lets someone use the work — ownership doesn't move. Only a clause that assigns the IP outright — 'all right, title, and interest, transferred' — actually hands it over. That gap is the design cost of English: a contract can read like it's transferring ownership, in warm confident prose, and still leave the work sitting with whoever created it. The check exists because that gap fools people.
Claude isn't judging whether the clause is good — it's running a written list, one item at a time, including the one that catches whether the clause actually assigns the IP or just licenses it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I need to know whether an IP clause in a contract actually transfers ownership or only grants a license. Here's the clause — paste it in. Before you give me a verdict, walk me through it step by step: does the clause use assignment language — 'assigns', 'all right, title, and interest, transferred' — or license language — 'grants a license to use'? What's the practical difference for who ends up owning the work? And if it's ambiguous, tell me the exact phrase that makes it ambiguous. Show your reasoning; don't just give me a yes or no. Go deeper: ask the same model to write you three example IP clauses that read like they transfer ownership but actually don't — and name the tell in each one.
